claims.text: Superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling strength is mediated by the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level can be tuned through compositional changes.
Nb is an element with strong intrinsic electron-phonon interactions.
Increasing Nb concentration in a Ti-rich HEA should increase the density of states at the Fermi level.
Increasing Nb concentration in a Ti-rich HEA should raise its superconducting critical temperature.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase, Ti-rich HEA without a dominant Nb-Ta matrix.
The Nb increase will be implemented by replacing some Ti or another less strongly coupled element.
The modified material will remain a fully disordered solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
Using identical melting, annealing, and cooling conditions for baseline and modified alloys will make compositional variation the attributable cause of observed superconducting changes.
Nb has a beneficial electronic structure for superconductivity.
Increasing Nb strengthens electron pairing by increasing the density of states at the Fermi level.
The Nb-enriched alloy should have a higher superconducting critical temperature than the Ti-rich baseline.
The Nb-enriched alloy should show a measurable change in electronic density of states relative to the baseline.
The original Ti-rich baseline has a lower critical temperature than a potential Nb-enriched variant.
The original Ti-rich baseline has a lower density of states at the Fermi level than a potential Nb-enriched variant.
The proposed mechanism is applicable only while the alloys remain disordered, single-phase solid solutions without extrinsic phase separation or ordering.
Disorder-induced scattering may counteract the superconducting benefit expected from stronger electron-phonon coupling.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes alloys that undergo phase separation or ordering, but the falsification rule treats observation of phase separation or ordering as falsification. Such an observation would place the material outside the stated applicability domain rather than directly refute the mechanism within that domain.
